newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Ericsson pins hopes on new handphone.
newsitem.headline: Ericsson pins hopes on new handphone.

text.p: Swedish telecommunications group Ericsson hopes its new mini GF788 handphone, launched this week, will help maintain its already large share of Asia's booming mobile market, senior company executives said on Friday.

Lars-Olof Pehrsson, regional director for Ericsson's cellular division, told Reuters his company had more than 30 percent of the US$5-10 billion sales of digital mobile phones in the Asia-Pacific region outside Japan last year.
In Singapore, Ericsson's share of new phone sales had reached an overwhelming 60 percent in recent months, up from just six or seven percent in 1994.
Pehrsson said his company's success had been largely based on its popular products, including its GF337 and GF388 phones, which had outsold their rivals in many markets.

But he said the company needed to work hard to maintain its market share and hoped its GF788 model, which at just 10 cm long and only 135 grams is one of the world's smallest phones, would help it do this.
"The competition is after us and to keep that position will be very difficult," Pehrsson said in an interview.

"If you have reached 60 percent you have to work much harder than anyone with half of that. If you have achieved your number one position, my goodness, everyone is after you, everyone is watching you," he said.
Sold in four colours and with numerous additional gimmicks, such as personalised ringing sounds, the toy-like GF788 is aimed at Asia's fashion-conscious newly rich.

"It's a fashion item today. Today it is a reflection of your personality, like your watch, or your spectacles," Pehrsson said. "We want people to say, 'Oh, look it's an Ericsson,' rather like people might say, "It's Armani'."

Ulf Mansson, head of sales and marketing at Ericsson's Asian cellular mobile phones division, said the company's new model should help it maintain its share of an Asian market growing faster than any other region in the world.
This year he expects a total of around 100 million new digital mobile phones of all brands to be sold worldwide, of which 40-45 million will be sold in Asia.
"We have more than a third of the Asian market outside Japan," Mansson told Reuters. "I would hope we could improve that market share with our new product."

"By the year 2000, analysts say there will be 500 million mobile phone sold worldwide. I think that is conservative. By the end of 1997, I think Asia will have passed Europe and the United States as the biggest single market," he said.
Pehrsson said Ericsson hoped the type of fashion styling used on the GF788 would help Ericsson enter the lucrative Japanese mobile phone market.
The company would move into Japan this year and hoped to become the second or third best seller by 2000, he said.

"We took a decision three or four years ago not to go into the Japanese market but to concentrate on outside Japan. Probably that was a good move. But today we are looking at the market and will enter the market later this year," he said.
"The Japanese market has grown faster than any other market in the world. It is a really terrific market place."
Pehrsson said he expected most growth for the company outside Japan to come from China and, in four or five years time, from India.
